newsitem.title: USA: U.S. fed cattle numbers at possible June 1 record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. fed cattle numbers at possible June 1 record.

text.p: U.S. cattle feeders actively put cattle on feed during May, which led to historically large and possibly record numbers of cattle on feed as of June 1, analysts said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department is expected to confirm the large cattle supplies on Friday in its monthly Cattle on Feed report, set for release at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT.

Analysts project the data will show cattle on feed in feedlots of 1,000-head-or-more capacity in the seven key states on June 1 at an average 113.2 percent of a year ago. Analysts' estimates ranged from 111.5 to 114.0 percent.

The higher end of estimates would be a record for the period since 1992 when the current series of reports began, and would be historically high even compared with reports comprised of previous methodology.
The previous record was about 8.2 million head on feed June 1, 1995. The high end of estimates would be about 8.3 million head.

Andy Gottschalk, LFG senior vice president said on-feed numbers are 60,000 head above the 1995 figure and if current data were adjusted to reflect the old series of reports, the on-feed number would be as large as in 1973.
Gottschalk estimated June 1 on-feed supplies at 113.9 percent.
"They are historically big and we will have plenty of cattle reaching market weight during the summer and fall period," Gottschalk said.

Analysts continue to estimate seven-state numbers while building historical data on the new 12-state part of the report. USDA made revisions to its seven-state report and introduced a 12-state report in January 1996.
May placement estimates averaged 117.2 percent of a year ago, ranging from 110.5 to 124.0 percent.

Analysts noted that placements look larger than they actually are because this year's numbers were being compared to an exceptionally low placement number last year when high corn prices curbed cattle feeders' interest.

"A year ago we had extremely high feed costs and it really caused some disruptions in placements and distorted the numbers. But the on-feed number is large," said Tom Tippens, chief executive officer of Professional Cattle Consultants Inc. He sees placements at 110.5 percent of a year ago.
"The percentages are deceptive, they don't necessarily tell the real story," Tippens said.
Given the large on-feed supply, analysts are looking for cash cattle prices to dip this summer and possibly into fall.
Gottschalk said he previously had projected fed cattle prices down to the $60 to $64 per cwt area but he now looks for prices at the low end of the range based on the large supply.
May marketings estimates for Friday's seven-state report averaged 99.0 percent of a year ago, ranging from 97.0 to 102.0 percent.

Feedlots scrambled to keep marketings current during May but with plentiful cattle supplies ahead, sales will need to continue brisk. How fast prices recover in the fall will depend on how aggressive summer marketings are, sources said.

"We have a lot of numbers to move through and cattle feeders are going to start coming under pressue for margins. If they hold back on their marketings because of that, we are going to back up cattle and that is going to stall any fall rally," Skold added.
